items.title: Accounting profit and economic profit measure different things
items.claim: A bakery reports £80,000 accounting profit. The owner could earn £50,000 in alternative employment and £15,000 by renting out the premises. What is the economic profit?
items.reveal:
Accounting profit deducts only explicit costs. Economic profit also deducts opportunity costs — the next-best foregone returns to the owner's time and assets. Here: £80,000 - £50,000 - £15,000 = £15,000.

A business with positive accounting profit but negative economic profit is destroying value relative to alternatives. The distinction was formalised by Alfred Marshall in his 'Principles of Economics' (1890).
items.why: A firm reporting profit on its income statement may still be the wrong use of the owner's resources. Accounting standards weren't designed to answer that question.

items.title: UK Supreme Court ruled Uber drivers were workers, not self-employed
items.claim: In February 2021, the UK Supreme Court ruled on the employment status of Uber drivers. What did it decide?

options.text: Drivers were correctly classified as self-employed
Drivers were 'workers' under UK law, entitled to minimum wage, paid holiday and pension auto-enrolment
Drivers were 'employees' with full unfair-dismissal rights
Uber was banned from operating in the UK

items.reveal:
The case ran from a 2016 Employment Tribunal decision to the Supreme Court. Lord Leggatt's judgment held that Uber's contract terms could not displace the reality of control: Uber set fares, terms, the rating system and routes.

Uber subsequently announced UK drivers would be paid minimum wage and pension contributions. The judgment did not give drivers full 'employee' status (no protection against unfair dismissal). Similar litigation has run in California, France and the Netherlands.
items.why: UK employment law has three statuses (employee, worker, self-employed). The 'worker' middle category was created in 1996; gig economy litigation has been the main test of where the line falls.

items.title: Small business survival rates are lower than commonly thought
items.claim: ONS UK Business Demography statistics consistently show what 5-year survival rate for new UK businesses?

options.text: Around 40% — roughly six in ten new UK businesses don't survive five years

items.reveal_title: Most new businesses don't make it
items.reveal:
ONS Business Demography data: of UK enterprises born in 2017, 39.6% survived to 2022. Year-1 survival is around 90%; the attrition is concentrated in years 2-5. SME failure causes (UK Federation of Small Businesses surveys) cluster around cash flow, late payment, and lack of management capacity.

Entrepreneurship narratives in business teaching focus on success stories. The base rate is more sobering and is one reason support programmes (start-up loans, mentoring) emphasise survival skills over growth.
items.why: Survivor bias in business case studies hides the failure rate. A textbook with only successful firms gives a misleading picture of what running a business actually involves.
